To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) a simple neural network agent trained to ground language in a visual environment can exhibit a number of developmental biases, including a bias to learn the meaning of words in the order they are presented, (2) these effects emerge from the agent's ability to learn a representation that is both semantically structured and context-dependent, and (3) the same representation can account for the observed biases in both the order of word learning and the order of learning to interpret syntactically complex instructions.

(i) the model learns a semantic representation that is similar in some key ways to human semantic representation, including the emergence of a bias towards learning the referents of concrete words; (ii) this bias is driven by a combination of a prior over word meanings that is biased towards concrete words, and a preference for learning the referents that are most likely to be relevant to the task; (iii) this bias is modulated by a preference for learning referents that are easy to learn;

(1) the learning agent displays a bias to learn words that are semantically coherent with its prior knowledge, (2) it displays a bias to interpret words that refer to objects that are semantically related to the objects that it already knows, and (3) it displays an effect of learning to interpret words that refers to objects that it already know, which is stronger when the words are semantically related.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of whether and how grounded language learning can be explained in terms of well-understood learning principles, and how this might inform future research in AI and psychology.
understanding and improving the learning mechanisms that enable language learning agents to learn to ground words and phrases.
understanding the learning dynamics and semantic representation of grounded language learning agents, in order to better understand how humans learn language.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
our work provides a better understanding of how neural network-based language learners learn to ground language.
the agent’s semantic representation is not only interpretable, but also highly similar to human semantics in terms of its structure, content, and development.
the agent learns to interpret linguistic instructions by building up a semantic representation in which the meanings of linguistic symbols are grounded in the visual world.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
grounded language learning agents are able to overcome the challenges that are also faced by humans in the early stages of language development.
grounded language learning is a complex and nuanced task for which there is no single best solution, but for which there is a clear set of principles governing how agents should learn.

grounded language learning agents can learn to interpret linguistic instructions as a first-person actor in a 3D world, and that the learning dynamics of these agents are consistent with the biases and effects observed in human infants.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the agent's learning is guided by a simple form of statistical inference, which is consistent with the idea that language learning is a process of statistical inference.

, in the absence of any explicit prior knowledge, a neural network-based agent can learn to interpret simple instructions in a way that is consistent with the way that infants learn their first words.

, while the neural network architecture and training procedure are critical for grounded language learning, the observed effects emerge from the interaction between these components and the task structure.
